Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Identifying Causal Effects in Experiments with Latent Treatments: An Instrumental Variable Approach

text.text: Psychological experiments target the causal effects of latent variables, which they cannot manipulate directly.
Researchers use manipulation checks to confirm that the latent variable changed, but then estimate the causal effect of the manipulation itself, not that of changes in the target latent variable.
We treat the manipulation as an instrumental variable (IV) for the latent treatment, measured by several items, and derive conditions under which the treatment's average causal effect is identified.
The resulting assumptions allow for some treatment-effect and loading heterogeneity, and are weaker than those most psychometric applications already make.
Because a latent treatment has no unit, the estimand is defined only once a scale is fixed.
We define two and work out their identification: an anchored estimand, per unit of one item, and a standardized estimand, per standard deviation of the latent treatment.
The latter is more familiar but requires more assumptions and, notably, does not transfer between experiments.
We show how to estimate both estimands with off-the-shelf SEM and IV software, and a simulation shows how the estimators behave in realistic samples when individual assumptions fail.
Because researchers design the manipulation and choose the items, we close with practical implications.
Psychologists and social scientists are interested in causal effects of changes in latent variables, such as psychological states, traits, or emotions.
These latent variables pose two problems for causal inference: latent variables cannot be observed, and, more consequentially, they cannot be manipulated directly in an experiment.
For example, to study how sadness X affects a financial decision Y , sadness must be manipulated by proxy, with an emotionally evocative film clip (Lerner et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For example, to study how sadness X affects a financial decision Y , sadness must be manipulated by proxy, with an emotionally evocative film clip <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Lerner et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The film clip Z is the experimental manipulation, but it is of no substantive interest in itself: it serves only to shift the target variable X, the emotional state observed via self-reported affect ratings.

The same structure recurs whenever a procedure is used to move a latent state: a stereotype-threat framing raises experienced threat (Steele & Aronson, 1995), an induced-compliance procedure provokes dissonance (Festinger & Carlsmith, 1959), the Trier Social Stress Test elevates stress (Kirschbaum et al., 1993), and an effortful task induces ego depletion (Baumeister et al., 1998).

text.text: In each case, the researcher randomizes Z but not X, so the study is not a classical experiment: observed changes between groups are due to Z, and this randomization does not rule out confounding of the X → Y relationship by unmeasured variables U .
Retrieving the target causal effect (the causal estimand) therefore requires further assumptions about how X, its measurement, and the instrument Z used to shift it are connected.
Knowing these necessary assumptions is vital, because experimenters have some control over design and measurement and can tailor both to make the assumptions plausible.

Psychological interventions Z can be characterized as indirect interventions (Junker & Grosz, 2026; Mathur, 2025), which places them in the general framework of instrumental variable (IV) identification, well established in the causal inference literature (Hernán & Robins, 2006; G. Imbens, 2014).

Imbens, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: IV approaches exploit the randomization of Z even though Z shifts X only partially.

Outside of psychology, such a source of exogenous variation (a lottery, a policy change, or assignment to a treatment arm in a randomized trial) is used to estimate treatment effects even though the treatment itself was not randomized.

In this sense, psychological experiments resemble randomized encouragement designs, common in medical trials with non-compliance, where participants can only be encouraged to take a treatment, but compliance is not enforced.
IV identification has received growing attention in the psychological literature, so far for manifest treatments (Grosz et al., 2024; Maydeu-Olivares et al., 2019; Student, 2026).

First, psychological variables cannot be measured directly: the latent treatment X is observed only through indicators I 1 , . . . , I J , each of which reflects X with error.

First, the LATE depends on the instrument: different instruments induce different rates of compliance and thus different estimands.
A sadness film and a sad autobiographical writing task move different people, so each identifies the effect of sadness on decision making in a different subpopulation.
Psychologists rarely care about effects tied to one particular manipulation; they use instruments to shift a target construct and want the effect of that construct on the outcome.
For the same reason, mediation effects of Z through X are not of substantive interest (Mathur, 2025).
text.formatted: For the same reason, mediation effects of Z through X are not of substantive interest <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Mathur, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the complier population is itself not identified: without further assumptions, no individual can be classified as a complier.
For continuous treatments such as psychological constructs, "compliers" are not even a well-defined group.
With continuous X, the LATE becomes a weighted average of heterogeneous effects whose weights depend on the instrument in ways that are hard to interpret substantively (Angrist et al., 1996).
text.formatted: With continuous X, the LATE becomes a weighted average of heterogeneous effects whose weights depend on the instrument in ways that are hard to interpret substantively <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Angrist et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Third, monotonicity is not plausible in psychological settings.
In medical trials it is defensible, because patients can typically access the treatment only if assigned to the treatment group.

In psychological experiments, participants in both groups can move their latent state up or down, and it is unreasonable to assume that everyone responds to the instrument in the same direction or not at all.
A film clip meant to induce sadness may leave some participants unmoved and strike others as absurd, cheering them up.
There are two possible conditions, each of which allows us to generalize immediately from the compliers to the population.

Under the first, everyone responds to Z in exactly the same way, that is, the effect of Z on X is constant and additive across individuals: the film clip makes every participant sadder by the same amount.
The instrument-induced variation in X is then homogeneous and there is no relevant non-complier subgroup to speak of.
Under the second, participants differ in how sad the clip makes them, but a given increase in sadness changes the financial decision Y by the same amount for everyone.
The complier-specific effect then coincides with the population ACE, and the IV estimate can be interpreted as the ACE.
Either condition suffices, and both are arguably strong and unrealistic, which is why the IV literature opted for different ways (see Box 1).
Yet both conditions hold simultaneously in an LSEM without interactions.
An LSEM takes Y to be linear in X and additionally restricts β Xi and β Y i to be constant across individuals.

This is a peculiar assumption in light of Figure 1, which posits that unmeasured confounders U exist and jointly influence both X and Y : financial strain may make participants sadder and more impatient on average, but it is not allowed to make them more responsive to the film or more swayed by their own sadness.

text.text: Many psychologists readily make these assumptions due to modeling convenience, because the standard LSEM encodes them by default.
While LSEMs are popular in psychological science, they are neither intuitive nor plausible through the lens of counterfactual causal inference.
We typically expect the effect of an intervention Z on X to vary substantially across individuals, and likewise expect the causal effect of X on Y to be modified by person-level characteristics.
In that sense, the LSEM encodes a very special case of homogeneity: all effect modification by unmeasured variables is ruled out by construction.
Recent work has shown that this "constant effect" assumption is stricter than necessary for point identification of the ACE (Hartwig et al., 2023; Wang & Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2018).

The main advantage of instrumental variables is that they tolerate confounding of the form X ← U → Y even when U is unobserved.

The Anchor-Metric Estimand: Fewer Assumptions, Transportable Across Z
The standardized latent estimand is natural from a psychometric perspective, but it is not always the most useful causal estimand.
Its unit is fixed by the variance of X, so the estimand depends on the distribution of the latent treatment.

This becomes a problem when effects are transported to settings in which X has a different variance: to populations that vary more in their sadness, or to designs in which another film clip or a different Z shifts sadness more strongly.
A sadder film makes one SD of sadness a larger dose, and so yields a larger reported effect.
Comparability across studies is a central aim of experimental design, and study-specific scales are a recognized obstacle to it (Fu & Green, 2026a).

text.text: Bias With a Contaminated Anchor

Psychological experiments do not directly manipulate a treatment variable X, which means that estimating the causal effect of X on Y is not guaranteed by design but requires additional assumptions: three classical IV assumptions that make Z a valid instrument and one assumption for the structural relationship between X and Y (NOSH).
If X is latent, its scale is not intrinsic and multiple estimands may be identified.
This paper developed strategies to identify two of those estimands.
Via exclusion restrictions, the effect of Z on any downstream variable, be it an indicator or the outcome, should run only via X (Assumptions 2 and 5).
Via uncorrelated-heterogeneity conditions, the person-level treatment effects and item loadings must be uncorrelated with first-stage β Xi (Assumptions 4(b) and 6(b)).
Our simulation study violated these assumptions one at a time and demonstrated the resulting bias.

Because latent variables have no inherent scale, causal effects of a latent X can be expressed in two main ways: via an intervention that shifts X by one SD, or per unit on the scale of an anchor item, I 0 .
Both estimands require the traditional IV identification Assumptions 1-4, yet they differ in the assumptions they require of the indicators.
The SD strategy recovers the loadings, and hence the latent variance, from the inter-item covariance structure, so Assumptions 5-8 must hold at every indicator in the model.
The choice between the two estimands is not only a question of which assumptions one is willing to defend: whenever θ SD is identified, a valid anchor necessarily exists.
The decision is more about which estimand is useful. θ SD is familiar but has a major problem: its unit is fixed by Var(X), which depends on instrument strength.
5 A stronger Z inflates Var(X) and yields a larger θ SD even when the causal effect is unchanged.

This matters especially in psychological experiments, where Z is only a vehicle for shifting X and is 5 Under Assumptions 5-8, the effect can also be expressed per SD of X within a single condition, such as the control condition (Z = 0).
This can be useful in two cases.

First, if the control manipulation has a constant effect on X, for instance no effect for any participant, the SD in the control condition is that of X in the unmanipulated population, and the effect can be transported.
Second, studies that share the same control manipulation Z = 0 can be compared even if their Z = 1 differs.

That standardized effects need care when compared across studies is well known (Pek & Flora, 2018). θ SD adds a further problem: it is standardized to an artificial experimental condition, for example the spread of X that one particular sad film produces, whereas causal questions in psychology usually concern X itself.

text.text: The effect is then comparable only with studies that shift X in a sufficiently similar way.
The anchor estimand, too, transports to other populations only if the anchor's average loading is the same there.
It does not depend on the instrument, however: given Assumptions 5 and 6 at the anchor, Z does not affect the anchor loading.
The SD estimand is the more appealing choice for a latent X that is measured with no clear anchor but with a variety of valid indicators, which differ from task to task or from study to study.
Cognitive tasks with a latent X such as memory or general ability are of this kind.
The anchor strategy fits the opposite case: it is appealing if few items are available and the same established items already recur across studies.
Personality research is one example, where a Big Five item can serve as the anchor.

The anchor strategy fits with trends that emphasize shorter scales (Allen et al., 2022; Eisele & Houben, 2026; Matthews et al., 2022), but some estimators can also use information of other items to gain efficiency, provided Assumptions 7 and 8 hold at those items.

text.text: Identification for both estimands requires that X is measured in the same way in both conditions of Z, which is why the assumptions made here resemble familiar assumptions about measurement invariance.

Measurement invariance is typically defined as a probability statement: among participants with the same value of the latent variable, the indicators must have the same joint distribution in both conditions, (I 1 , . . . , I J ) ⊥ ⊥ Z | X (Meredith, 1993).
text.formatted: Measurement invariance is typically defined as a probability statement: among participants with the same value of the latent variable, the indicators must have the same joint distribution in both conditions, (I 1 , . . . , I J ) ⊥ ⊥ Z | X <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Meredith, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: This is usually discussed as a prerequisite for comparing latent variables across populations; here, only the experimental conditions Z ∈ {0, 1} are compared.

Recent work has recognized that traditional measurement invariance assumptions demand far more than most analyses require, and more than most analysts are willing to defend (Rohrer & Paulewicz, 2025; Sterner et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent work has recognized that traditional measurement invariance assumptions demand far more than most analyses require, and more than most analysts are willing to defend <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Rohrer & Paulewicz, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Sterner et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: They hold each indicator to be exogenous to every variable except the latent variable it measures, with loadings constant across persons.
A factor model this restrictive trivially satisfies the conditions derived here, but assumes much more than IV analyses typically do.
Suitable tests of measurement invariance, like multi-group SEMs, fail if any of Assumptions 5, 6 or 8 is violated, provided the other items are invariant.

Yet they can also fail when the effect is identified: θ I 0 does not require Assumption 8 at the anchor, and heterogeneous loadings make the test of strict invariance fail even when they are unrelated to X and Z and thus satisfy Assumption 6(b).
This general understanding of measurement invariance is therefore not necessary for identification, and, more consequentially, a failing test does not show which assumption could be violated.
Stating measurement invariance causally gives an opportunity to explain why invariance fails and to account for it in the analysis (Sterner et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Stating measurement invariance causally gives an opportunity to explain why invariance fails and to account for it in the analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Sterner et al., 2024)</ref>.

Imbens & Angrist, 1994): state the causal estimand of interest, then find the minimal requirements under which it can be estimated from data.

text.text: Accurate measurement of X that is comparable across other subgroups, such as fully transportable loadings, is at best collateral.
The indicators are part of the same causal system as Z, X and Y , and the assumptions they must satisfy follow from the estimand and its identification strategy.
The causal inference literature states assumptions about the causal substance, independent of estimation or modeling technique, and this makes those assumptions easier to evaluate.

In the running example, Assumption 6(b) can be stated with reference to features of the experimental design: it fails if participants who are moved more by the film also use the sadness rating more extremely, for instance because both depend on emotional expressivity.
Stated this way, the assumption names a pre-treatment moderator that can be measured, checked and adjusted for.
In contrast, assumptions that are stated about the model, such as "constant loadings" or (I 1 , . . . , I J ) ⊥ ⊥ Z | X, offer no such handle.
The identification results presented here rest on assumptions that psychometric applications routinely make, often in a stronger form.
Still, they are restrictive and should be stated carefully in practice.
Two of them are linearity requirements that could be relaxed.

Linearity of X → Y (Assumption 4(a)) is probably a minor concern, because the measurement error common in psychological studies tends to make nonlinear effects look linear anyway (Jacobucci & Grimm, 2020).
text.formatted: Linearity of X → Y (Assumption 4(a)) is probably a minor concern, because the measurement error common in psychological studies tends to make nonlinear effects look linear anyway <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Jacobucci & Grimm, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Linearity of X → I 0 (Assumption 6(a)) matters more in practice, because it restricts the anchor strategy to items that can be treated as continuous.
That excludes the binary and ordinal item response models that dominate psychological measurement (Van Der Linden & Hambleton, 1997), which are nonlinear by construction.

text.text: Our simulation study had a limited scope and did not cover a range of realistic scenarios.
The scenarios check the theoretical results and are no substitute for a design or power analysis.
Each scenario violates a single assumption at moderate strength, with a strong instrument, a large causal effect, and high loadings.
Applied studies likely face several violations at once.
Weaker instruments, smaller effects, and lower loadings make every estimator less precise.
The Anchor-Wald estimator is most affected, since it rests on a single item.
The sample size a study needs, and the estimator that performs best in it, depend on all of these parameters jointly.

A realistic power analysis therefore would need plausible values for each parameter, including the strength of every source of confounding and the combinations in which these sources are likely to co-occur.

Future work should evaluate the estimators in more realistic scenarios and address the bias-variance trade-off of adding more items: each additional item may gain efficiency but may also add confounding.
Throughout, Y was treated as unidimensional or manifest for simplicity.
The framework extends directly to a latent or multidimensional Y , for example by adding an indicator of Y to the Wald ratio.

However, the approach does not generalize to multidimensional treatment variables X. Because each facet can be changed separately, the treatment can be changed in several ways, which makes the estimand harder to define.
If the facets of X differ in their effect on Y , it is unclear which change the causal estimand refers to, and (causal) consistency between data and estimand fails (Junker & Grosz, 2026).

text.text: In our example, sadness that comes with a sense of loss may trigger a search for immediate reward, which shifts financial decisions (Lerner et al., 2013); sadness that comes with a sense of personal failure might not.

text.text: A causal estimand that takes broadly defined "sadness" as X is then ill-defined.
Treatment variables should therefore be sufficiently unidimensional.
This makes (causal) consistency more plausible and the exclusion restrictions (Assumptions 2 and 5) easier to state.
The assumptions laid out above are strong and will not hold perfectly in applied settings.
That is precisely why they are worth stating.
A psychological experiment is constructed by the experimenter, who usually chooses both the manipulation Z and the indicators I j from several candidates.
The assumptions are therefore design targets and can be made more plausible beforehand.
IV applications in economics and epidemiology are often limited to natural experiments outside the researcher's control.
In psychology, researchers can choose their Z according to desirable properties: First, the instrument Z should have a strong effect on X.
Weak instruments lead at best to wide, uninformative confidence intervals, and at worst they amplify bias whenever any of the other assumptions is even slightly violated (Hernán & Robins, 2020).
text.formatted: Weak instruments lead at best to wide, uninformative confidence intervals, and at worst they amplify bias whenever any of the other assumptions is even slightly violated <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Hernán & Robins, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the exclusion restrictions on Z must hold: any causal effect of Z on Y , or on any indicator I j , that is not fully mediated by X is problematic.
Notably this is an assumption about unmeasured paths, such as indirect Z → U → I j , outside the model.
Third, Z should work through mechanisms unrelated to moderators of the X → Y relationship.
A sad film depicting financial hardship moves financially strained participants most, and they are plausibly also the ones whose monetary choices react most to sadness.
A sad film without financial content decouples the two and makes NOSH far more defensible.
Unfortunately, psychological methods offer no clear, empirically validated recipes for ensuring that these assumptions hold.
Instead, there are many compelling examples of likely violations.

Violations of IV assumptions behave differently from violations in traditional confounder-adjustment methods: they can amplify bias, so that a simple OLS estimate may be biased and still land closer to the ACE than an IV estimate in which a single assumption fails (Hernán & Robins, 2020).

text.text: The exclusion restrictions, that Z affects both Y and I j only via X, are probably the most critical assumptions; but they plague any causal inference in psychological experiments, due to their indirect nature (Eronen, 2020; Mathur, 2025).

text.text: In contrast, heterogeneous effects and loadings likely matter less in practice, but allowing them comes for free.
The NOSH assumptions stated here generalize constant-effect assumptions and permit arbitrary individual-level heterogeneity in both the Z → X and the X → Y relation.

This gives applied researchers a more transparent target: instead of assuming away all heterogeneity, they are asked to reason about whether the variables that make individuals more (or less) responsive to the instrument are also likely to make them more (or less) susceptible to the treatment effect.

If such moderators are plausible and measured, they can be included in the treatment and outcome models, relaxing the burden placed on the unmeasured remainder of U and making the homogeneity assumption more plausible.
From a practical standpoint, this does not make the models more complicated.
If the ACE is the target, the heterogeneity does not need its own parameter and can remain in the error term.

A study can still be planned under optimistic parametric conditions, for example by taking our clean baseline scenario and additionally assuming a standard LSEM, which takes effects and loadings to be constant.
This makes plausible parameter values for a power analysis easier to manage.

The analysis can then use the same model: in our simulation, SEM-IV, which fixes the loadings, remains unbiased when effects and loadings vary, provided the remaining assumptions hold, because the loading variance is simply absorbed into the item error.

The proposed identification strategies therefore do not require new estimation techniques: off-the-shelf software such as lavaan suffices, and the model settings differ from routine practice by a single scaling constraint.
What may change is the target quantity, and studies that report SD scaled estimands could also report anchored estimands.
The effect of sadness on financial decisions, for example, would be reported both per scale point of a single sadness rating and in units of the latent construct itself.
The anchor estimand is identified under less stringent assumptions.
It is not "the effect" of sadness in the abstract way that researchers may have hoped to report, but it is the effect they are better equipped to identify, defend and compare.
Thus, to quote Angrist and Pischke (2009, p. 83): "Sometimes You Get What You Need."

text.text: In the first approach, the latent variable is operationalized by estimating a Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) model and extracting factor scores.
These scores are then treated as a manifest variable in a standard two-stage least squares regression.
While computationally simple, this method treats the factor scores as observed in the second stage.

The uncertainty of the estimated loadings, which fix the scale of the scores, is not.
